posts.title: What affects the cost of a home EV charger installation?
posts.excerpt: No two installations are quite the same. These are the factors that move the price of a home EV charger up or down, and how to compare quotes fairly.
posts.cover_image_alt: A wall-mounted EV charger on a brick wall being used
posts.seo_title: What Affects the Cost of a Home EV Charger Installation?
posts.seo_description: The charger, the cable run, your fuse box and your property all affect the price of a home EV charger installation. Learn what drives the cost.
posts.body:
Ask three installers for a price and you may well get three different numbers. That is not necessarily a sign that anyone is overcharging: the cost of fitting a home EV charger depends on your property as much as on the charger itself. Knowing what drives the price makes it much easier to compare quotes like for like.

## The charger itself

Chargers vary in price with their power output, whether they are tethered or untethered, and the features they offer, such as solar integration, load balancing or app control. Some installers supply the charger as part of a package; others will fit one you have already bought. Check which applies before you compare quotes.

## How far the charger is from your fuse box

The biggest variable is usually the cable run. A charger on the outside wall of a garage that also houses your consumer unit (fuse box) needs only a short cable. A charger on a post at the end of a driveway, or on a detached garage, may need a much longer run, armoured cable and groundworks such as trenching or drilling through thick walls.

## Your consumer unit and electricity supply

An EV charger needs its own circuit with suitable protection. If your consumer unit is old or has no spare space, it may need upgrading. Your installer will also check your main fuse rating and how much power your home already uses, and may recommend load management so the charger never overloads your supply.

Some homes share a supply cable with a neighbour, known as a "looped" supply. Your installer will tell you if your network operator needs to separate it before the charger can be connected.

## Earthing and safety protection

Outdoor charge points must be protected against certain earthing faults. Many modern chargers include this protection built in; others need extra equipment, such as an earth rod. This is a safety requirement, not an optional extra, so make sure every quote includes it.

## What a good quote includes

When you compare quotes, check that each one covers:

- the charger make and model, or confirms you are supplying your own
- the cable route and length, and any groundworks
- any consumer unit or protection upgrades
- notifying your network operator and, where required, Building Control
- testing, certification and setting up the charger app with you
- the warranty on both the charger and the workmanship

> **Tip:** a survey, in person or from photos and a short video call, gives you a firmer price than an estimate made without seeing your property.

posts.title: Tethered or untethered? Choosing the right home EV charger
posts.excerpt: A tethered charger has its cable permanently attached; an untethered one has a socket. Here is how to decide which suits your car and your driveway.
posts.cover_image_alt: A driver connecting a charging cable to an electric car
posts.seo_title: Tethered vs Untethered EV Chargers: Which Should You Choose?
posts.seo_description: Tethered or untethered? Compare convenience, compatibility and connectors to choose the right home EV charger for your car and your driveway.
posts.body:
One of the first decisions when you choose a home EV charger is whether you want it **tethered** or **untethered**. Both charge your car in exactly the same way. The difference is the cable, and that affects convenience, appearance and how future-proof your charger is.

## What is a tethered charger?

A tethered charger has its charging cable permanently attached. You take the plug off the holder, connect it to your car and you are charging. Many drivers find this the most convenient choice for everyday use, especially if they charge most nights.

## What is an untethered charger?

An untethered charger has a socket instead of a fixed cable. You plug in your own cable each time, usually the one that came with your car. The unit itself looks neater and more compact on the wall.

## Side by side

| | Tethered | Untethered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cable | Permanently attached | You use your own cable |
| Everyday use | Unhook and plug in | Take the cable out of the boot each time |
| Compatibility | Fixed connector type | Any car, with the right cable |
| Appearance | Cable coiled on or around the unit | Compact socket, no loose cable |

## Which connector does your car use?

Most electric cars sold in the UK today use a **Type 2** connector for home charging, but some older models use **Type 1**. If you choose a tethered charger, make sure its connector matches your car, and think about whether the next car in your household will use the same one. An untethered charger avoids the question: you simply use the right cable.

## How much power do you need?

Most home chargers in the UK are rated at around 7 kW, which suits the single-phase electricity supply found in most homes. Faster 22 kW chargers need a three-phase supply, which few homes have. Your installer will confirm what your supply can support.

## So which should you choose?

- Choose **tethered** if convenience matters most and everyone in your household has a car with the same connector.
- Choose **untethered** if you want a neater look, have more than one type of car, or expect to change car in the next few years.

Not sure? Mention it when you [request your free quotes](/get-quotes/) and your installer can recommend a charger that suits your car and your driveway.

posts.title: What to expect on EV charger installation day
posts.excerpt: From the safety checks to the handover, here is what happens when a qualified installer fits your EV charger, and the documents you should receive.
posts.cover_image_alt: An electrician working on a consumer unit
posts.seo_title: What to Expect on EV Charger Installation Day
posts.seo_description: A step-by-step guide to a home EV charger installation: the survey, the work on the day, testing, the handover and the certificates you should receive.
posts.body:
Having an EV charger fitted is usually a straightforward job, and knowing what will happen makes the day easier to plan. Here is what to expect from a qualified installer, from the first visit to the handover.

## Before the day

Your installer will want to understand your property before they arrive. Many carry out a survey, either in person or from photos of your fuse box, electricity meter and the place you want the charger.

They will also confirm the charger model, the cable route and any extra work, such as a consumer unit upgrade. In most cases they notify your electricity network operator about the new charger, and some installations need the network operator's approval first.

## On the day

A typical installation follows these steps:

1. **Safety checks.** The installer inspects your existing installation and agrees the exact charger position with you.
2. **Power off.** Your electricity is switched off for part of the job, so plan around it if you work from home.
3. **Fixing the charger.** The unit is mounted on the wall or on a post.
4. **Running the cable.** A dedicated cable is run from your consumer unit to the charger, through walls or underground if needed.
5. **Connecting and protecting.** The new circuit is connected with the right protection devices, and earthing measures are put in place.
6. **Testing.** The installer tests the circuit to make sure it is safe and meets the wiring regulations.
7. **Commissioning.** The charger is switched on, connected to your Wi-Fi or mobile signal, and set up in its app.

Most straightforward installations are finished within a day. Longer cable runs or groundworks can take longer.

## The handover

Before they leave, a good installer will show you how to use the charger and its app, including how to schedule charging for cheaper off-peak hours. You should receive:

- an Electrical Installation Certificate for the new circuit
- confirmation that the work has been registered with Building Control where required, usually through the installer's Competent Person Scheme
- the charger's warranty details and any workmanship guarantee

Keep these documents safe: you may need them when you sell your home or make a warranty claim.

posts.title: Smart charging rules explained: what they mean for your home charger
posts.excerpt: Home chargers sold in Great Britain must be smart. Here is what the rules require, and how you stay in control of when your car charges.
posts.cover_image_alt: A homeowner checking a charging app next to a wall charger
posts.seo_title: Smart Charging Rules Explained for Home EV Chargers
posts.seo_description: What the Smart Charge Points Regulations mean for your home EV charger: default off-peak settings, randomised delay, security and staying in control.
posts.body:
If you are buying a home EV charger in Great Britain, it has to be a **smart** charger. The Electric Vehicles (Smart Charge Points) Regulations 2021 set out what private charge points must be able to do. Here is what that means for you in practice.

## Why the rules exist

Millions of cars charging at the same time in the early evening would put a heavy load on the electricity network. Smart chargers can shift charging to quieter times, which helps keep the grid stable and can make charging cheaper for you.

## What a smart charger must do

In short, a compliant home charger must:

- be able to send and receive information, so it can respond to signals and change when and how fast it charges
- come with default settings that avoid charging at peak times, which you can accept or change
- include a randomised delay, so lots of chargers do not all switch on at exactly the same moment
- meet security requirements that protect the charger and your data
- let you see information about the electricity you use

## You stay in control

The rules do not stop you charging when you need to. You can change the default schedule and override it whenever you want to charge straight away. Most chargers let you do this from an app.

## Getting the most from smart charging

Many energy suppliers offer tariffs designed for electric car owners, with cheaper electricity overnight. Pairing one with a smart charger means your car can charge automatically during the cheapest hours. Some chargers can also use surplus power from solar panels.

## What it means when you buy

Reputable installers only fit compliant chargers, so this should be taken care of for you. If you already own a charger, it is worth asking your installer to confirm it meets the rules before they fit it.

> These rules apply in England, Scotland and Wales. Check with your installer if your property is in Northern Ireland.

Want to understand the wider rules for electrical work at home? Read our guide to [UK electrical safety and regulations](/electrical-safety-regulations/).

posts.title: How to choose a qualified EV charger installer
posts.excerpt: Accreditations, insurance, certificates and clear quotes: the checks that help you choose a qualified EV charger installer with confidence.
posts.cover_image_alt: A qualified electrician at work in a home
posts.seo_title: How to Choose a Qualified EV Charger Installer
posts.seo_description: Seven checks to make before you hire an EV charger installer, from Competent Person Scheme registration and insurance to certificates and reviews.
posts.body:
An EV charger is a permanent, high-power electrical installation, so who fits it matters. These are the checks worth making before you choose an installer.

## 1. A Competent Person Scheme registration

Electricians registered with a Competent Person Scheme, such as **NICEIC** or **NAPIT**, are assessed regularly and can self-certify that their work meets the Building Regulations. Ask which scheme your installer belongs to and check their registration on the scheme's website.

Find out what each one means in our guide to [electrician accreditations](/electrician-accreditations/).

## 2. Experience with EV chargers

EV charger installations have their own requirements, from earthing arrangements to network operator notifications. Ask how many chargers the installer fits, which brands they are approved to install, and whether they can show you examples of similar jobs.

## 3. Grant authorisation, if you need it

If you plan to use a government grant towards your charger, the installer usually has to be authorised under the relevant OZEV scheme. Check the current rules on GOV.UK before you book.

## 4. Insurance

A professional installer should hold public liability insurance. It is reasonable to ask for proof.

## 5. A clear, written quote

A good quote names the charger, describes the cable route and any extra work, and states the total price including VAT. Be cautious of vague quotes or a price given without any questions about your property.

## 6. Certificates and warranty

Make sure the installer will give you an Electrical Installation Certificate and arrange Building Regulations compliance where required. Ask how long the charger warranty lasts and whether the workmanship is guaranteed.

## 7. Reviews from real customers

Reviews tell you how an installer communicates, whether they turn up on time and how tidy they are. On PickASparky, reviews come only from customers who were matched with the installer through a quote request.

posts.title: Getting ready for a home EV charger: a homeowner's checklist
posts.excerpt: A little preparation helps installers quote accurately and makes installation day go smoothly. Work through this checklist before you request quotes.
posts.cover_image_alt: An electric car charging from a post-mounted charger
posts.seo_title: Home EV Charger Checklist: How to Prepare for Installation
posts.seo_description: Parking, fuse box photos, Wi-Fi signal, permissions and your car's connector: a simple checklist to prepare for a home EV charger installation.
posts.body:
A little preparation helps installers give you an accurate quote and makes installation day go smoothly. Work through this checklist before you request quotes.

## Your parking and the charger position

- **Off-street parking.** A home charger needs a driveway, garage or private parking space next to your property. Trailing a cable across a pavement is not a safe option.
- **Where you will park.** Think about which side of the car the charging port is on and where the cable will reach most easily.
- **Wall or post.** Decide whether the charger can go on the house or garage wall, or whether it needs a post near the parking space.

## Your electrics

- **Find your fuse box.** Take a clear photo of your consumer unit with the cover open, if it is safe to do so, and another of your electricity meter.
- **Measure the distance.** Roughly how far is it, and through how many walls, from the fuse box to where you want the charger?
- **Mobile or Wi-Fi signal.** Smart chargers need a connection. Check the signal where the charger will go.

## Permissions

- **Do you own the property?** Tenants will need their landlord's permission, and leaseholders may need consent from the freeholder or management company.
- **Planning.** In most cases a home charger does not need planning permission, but listed buildings, conservation areas and flats can have extra rules. Check with your local planning authority if you are unsure.

## Your car and how you charge

- **Your car's connector.** Most cars sold in the UK today use a Type 2 connector, but check yours, especially if you are choosing a tethered charger.
- **Your tariff.** An energy tariff designed for electric cars can make overnight charging much cheaper.
- **Future plans.** A second electric car, solar panels or a home battery may change which charger is the best fit.

## Ready to compare quotes?

With this information to hand, our six quick questions take a couple of minutes. [Get up to 5 free quotes](/get-quotes/) from vetted installers who cover your postcode.
